analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to spend at least 90% of premiums on actual medical care, with rebates otherwise.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Health Committee: referred on September 30, 2009, it received no hearing, no vote, and no further action before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar insurers from selling coverage unless at least 90 cents of every premium dollar went to medical care for patients, rather than to overhead, salaries, or profit. Insurers falling short would have to rebate the difference to their customers. It was referred to the Senate Health Committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy or get health insurance. The bill would force insurers to deliver more of each premium as actual medical care or refund the shortfall, and to report standardized data so regulators and customers could see where premium dollars actually went.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a health insurance issuer from offering coverage unless it demonstrates a medical loss ratio of at least 90%, meaning 90% of premium revenue must go to medical care.

Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to set a uniform definition and calculation methodology for the ratio, taking into account activities like chronic disease management and quality assurance.
Requires issuers, starting in plan year 2011, to report the data HHS needs to check compliance, and to develop standardized reporting elements by December 31, 2010.
Requires issuers whose coverage falls below the 90% ratio in a plan year to provide rebates to enrollees, with regulations and penalties for enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, whose overhead and profit margins would be capped: any premium dollar not spent on patient care above 10% would have to be rebated to customers or the coverage could not be sold at all.

drawbacks.text: A single 90% floor applies to every plan, large or small; smaller insurers and plans with higher fixed administrative costs would have the hardest time meeting it, and some could leave markets where they compete, reducing choices for customers in those states.

The ratio is calculated after allowing for activities like disease management and quality assurance, so the effectiveness of the 90% floor would depend heavily on how HHS defined those allowances; a generous definition could let substantial overhead count as 'medical' spending.
Rebates go back to enrollees only after the plan year ends, not through lower premiums up front, so customers get money back rather than never overpaying in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and easy to understand: premium dollars tracked and mostly spent on care, with refunds when they are not. The costs are real but manageable — the main risks are that the definition HHS writes could blunt the standard, and that small plans could struggle to comply. The bill leans on the regulator to make it work, which is a fair criticism but not a fatal design flaw for a bill whose purpose is a floor, not a ceiling, on care spending.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health Committee, and that is where it stayed — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Al Franken introduced the bill on September 30, 2009, joined by original cosponsors including Senators Rockefeller, Whitehouse, and Sanders, during the months when Congress was writing the Affordable Care Act.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the bill's history: the committee took up no hearing or vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended.
The bill attracted six cosponsors — five Senate Democrats and the Senate's one Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers were better off: they never faced the 90% requirement or its rebates. When Congress did set medical loss ratio standards months later in the Affordable Care Act, it chose weaker levels — 80% for individual plans and 85% for group plans — than this bill's 90%.

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring a 90% medical loss ratio and referred it to the Senate Health Committee.

for.name: Sens. Jay Rockefeller and Sheldon Whitehouse

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Tom Harkin)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill after its referral on September 30, 2009; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the bill's support came entirely from progressive Democrats and the Senate's Independent, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would cap what insurers keep for overhead and profit at 10% of premiums and force refunds of anything above that, directly cutting into their margins. Its gain to ordinary customers — more premium dollars as care — is the insurers' loss.
